analyst:
Kansas enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a No. 4 seed in the East Region and is slated to open Friday, March 20, 2026 against No. 13 California Baptist. The selection bracket listed Kansas at 23-10 overall entering the field. Kansas finished the regular season 22-9 and 11-6 in Big 12 play as of the March 4 team notes, then added postseason results to reach 23-10 by Selection Sunday. Kansas averaged 75.6 points per game, allowed 68.8, shot 45.7% from the floor, 35.1% from three, and owned a +6.8 scoring margin; in league play, those numbers tightened to 75.4 scored and 72.9 allowed, which fits the eye test of a team that has been more rugged than fluid for long stretches. Kansas also averaged 38.6 rebounds and 14.4 assists per game overall, while opponents shot just 38.5% from the field and 29.8% from three against the Jayhawks. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/6bcf0716a22296d27aa9c253cb07fd21?utm_source=openai))

Offensively, this is still a Bill Self half-court team first. The numbers point to an inside-out structure built around rim pressure, post seals, and second-side creation rather than pure tempo: Kansas shoots 77.2% at the foul line, gets 14.5 made free throws per game, and rebounds at 38.6 per game, while its top frontcourt finisher, Flory Bidunga, shoots 63.7% from the floor. In practical terms, Kansas has leaned on post feeds to Bidunga, duck-ins from the dunker spot, horns-style actions with two big bodies at the elbows, and ball-screen creation for Darryn Peterson and Melvin Council Jr. The TCU game on January 6 is the clearest example of the offense’s ceiling and its shape: Kansas scored 104 points in overtime, Peterson had 32, Council handed out eight assists, and the Jayhawks attempted 40 free throws. Against Baylor on January 16, Peterson scored 26 and Bidunga grabbed 11 boards in an 80-62 win, another example of Kansas getting star-guard creation plus interior finishing. Against Arizona on February 9, with Peterson out, Kansas adjusted by flattening the offense into more direct drives and paint touches for Council, Bidunga, and Bryson Tiller; the result was 82 points against the nation’s then-No. 1 team. Kansas is not a beautiful volume-assist offense every night, but when it is right, Self gets touches to the lane first and lets the game grow from there. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/6/KUMBB_Kansas_State2.pdf))

The specific offensive tendencies show up in who finishes possessions. Peterson is the primary late-clock shot maker and mismatch hunter; he averaged 20.5 points per game through February 8 and 19.5 by March 4, while still shooting 38.5% from three by the later team notes. Council is the table-setter, leading Kansas with 150 assists and posting a 2.78 assist-to-turnover ratio, fifth in the Big 12. Bidunga is the vertical spacer and post finisher, averaging 13.8 points, 9.2 rebounds, and 2.7 blocks by March 4. Tre White supplies slashing and catch-and-shoot balance, averaging 14.0 points and 6.8 rebounds by March 4, while Bryson Tiller gives them a face-up four who can slip screens, crash, and finish. A traditional scout would call the offense “first-option physical”: post touches, elbow initiation, staggered actions to free a scorer, and guards who are expected to make hard downhill reads instead of overpassing. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/6/KUMBB_Kansas_State2.pdf))

Defensively, Kansas has looked more trustworthy than its offense. The statistical backbone is strong: opponents shot 38.5% overall and 29.8% from three, and in league play Kansas still held teams to 39.9% overall. The front line drives that identity. Bidunga led the Big 12 with 80 blocks and ranked third nationally at 2.67 blocks per game as of March 6; Tiller added 42 blocks. That gives Self real back-line eraser ability, so Kansas can pressure the ball with more confidence than last season’s groups. The Jayhawks want to shrink the floor, keep the ball out of the middle, and contest at the rim with length rather than gamble recklessly; Council led the team with 33 steals, but this is not a turnover-forcing, all-out denial unit. It is a shell-defense team with hard help, rim protection, and disciplined closeouts. The January 13 blowout of No. 2 Iowa State is the best single-game proof: Kansas held the Cyclones to 63 points, 37% shooting, and a season low in scoring, with Iowa State reaching its average in turnovers by halftime while shooting just 24% in the first half. Kansas also beat Houston 69-56 on February 23, another game that validated the defensive ceiling against a high-level half-court opponent. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/6/KUMBB_Kansas_State2.pdf))

Self’s coaching philosophy remains old-school Kansas basketball: defend first, own the glass, get paint touches, and trust experience and matchup manipulation late. His in-game adjustment history this season gives concrete examples. Against Arizona on February 9, with Peterson ruled out late, Self shifted usage to Council and Bidunga and rode Tiller’s scoring; Kansas erased an 11-point deficit and won 82-78, with Council and Bidunga scoring 23 each and Tiller adding 18. Against Texas Tech on February 2, Kansas trailed by nine with six minutes left, then closed on a 14-2 run to win 64-61; Peterson hit two threes in the final 1:20 for his only field goals of the second half, showing Self’s willingness to simplify late offense into star shot-making. Against Arizona State on March 3, Kansas played its first half under chaos after Self was ejected with just over six minutes left in the half; the Jayhawks shot only 21.1% in the first half, yet still rallied and cut the game to two late before losing 70-60. Even in defeat, that game showed the team’s ability to respond structurally after disruption. ([www2.ljworld.com](https://www2.ljworld.com/sports/ku-mens-basketball/2026/feb/09/quick-recap-down-goes-no-1-ku-topples-arizona-82-78/))

Clutch and late-game execution is one of the swing variables for this team, but the documented record is better than the broad narrative suggests. Kansas was 5-1 in games decided by five points or less or overtime after beating Arizona on February 9. The ledger includes a 77-76 overtime win at NC State on December 13, when Melvin Council Jr. scored 36 points and nine threes and also fed Bidunga for the go-ahead dunk with 51.9 seconds left in OT. It includes the 104-100 overtime win over TCU on January 6, powered by Peterson’s 32 points. It includes the 64-61 road win at No. 13 Texas Tech on February 2, when Peterson hit those two late threes. And it includes the 82-78 win over No. 1 Arizona on February 9, sealed by Bidunga’s block with 17 seconds left and late free throws from White and Council. The concern is that the bad late-game versions have also been ugly: Kansas lost at UCF 81-75 on January 3, got run off the floor late by Cincinnati 84-68 on February 21 at Allen Fieldhouse, and lost 70-60 at Arizona State on March 3 after digging too deep an early hole. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/KUMBB_Arizona_State.pdf))

The key players define the tournament ceiling. Peterson is the headliner and likely first-round NBA talent; by February 8 he averaged 20.5 points, 1.7 assists, and shot 48.9% overall and 41.9% from three, then sat at 19.5 points and 38.5% from three by March 4. His standout moments include 32 against TCU on January 6, 26 in the loss at UCF on January 3, 26 against Baylor on January 16, 23 at Oklahoma State on February 18, and the closing barrage at Texas Tech on February 2. Bidunga is the two-way anchor: 13.8 points, 9.2 rebounds, 2.7 blocks, 63.7% shooting, 80 total blocks. He posted 23 and 10 against Arizona, 21 and 10 at Kansas State, 17 and 10 against Utah, and 18 and 12 even in the home loss to Cincinnati. Council is the heartbeat guard: 13.3 points, 5.0 assists, team-best 150 assists, and 33 steals. His 36-point, nine-three outburst at NC State was the loudest example, and he also scored 23 against Arizona. White has become essential as a secondary scorer and rebounder; he scored 23 against Houston, 19 with 10 rebounds against Iowa State, and 15 rebounds at Colorado. Tiller is the glue frontcourt piece at 8.5 points, 6.0 rebounds, and 42 blocks; he scored 21 against BYU and 18 in the Arizona upset. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/2/8/KUMBB_Arizona_notes.pdf))

The notable wins are real and instructive. Kansas beat Tennessee 81-76 on November 26, beat Missouri 80-60 on December 7, won at NC State 77-76 in overtime on December 13, hammered No. 2 Iowa State 84-63 on January 13, beat Baylor 80-62 on January 16, won at No. 13 Texas Tech 64-61 on February 2, beat No. 1 Arizona 82-78 on February 9, and then held Houston to 56 in a 69-56 win on February 23. Those wins reveal the formula: when Kansas defends at a top-15 level, wins the paint, and gets enough shot creation from Peterson/Council/White, it can beat protected-seed caliber teams. The losses reveal the opposite. UConn beat Kansas 61-56 on December 2 in a grinder that exposed offensive limitations. West Virginia beat Kansas 86-75 on January 10, showing vulnerability when the game becomes whistle-heavy and messy. Iowa State beat Kansas 74-56 on February 14, exposing how the offense can stall on the road against pressure. Cincinnati’s 84-68 win in Lawrence on February 21 showed that if Kansas gets spread out defensively and loses the glass/transition battle, Allen Fieldhouse does not save it. Arizona then returned the favor with an 84-61 win on February 28, and Arizona State’s 70-60 win on March 3 underlined the danger of slow starts and thin-margin offense. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/6/KUMBB_Kansas_State2.pdf))

As for NCAA Tournament history, Self’s résumé is obviously elite. Kansas notes list him with two national titles at KU, and his official Kansas bio states that in his first trip to the Final Four in 2008, Kansas won the national championship; he later won a second title in 2022. Self also took Kansas to Final Fours in 2012 and 2018, and his broader tournament résumé includes deep runs at prior stops. At Kansas specifically, his round-by-round history includes reaching the Elite Eight in 2004, 2011, 2016, 2017, 2023, and 2024; Final Fours in 2008, 2012, and 2018; national runner-up in 2012; and national championships in 2008 and 2022. That matters in this specific bracket because Kansas is not a vintage juggernaut, but it is the kind of four-seed nobody enjoys preparing for: high-major size, elite rim protection, a lottery-level shot creator, and a coach with a long record of surviving the first weekend and adjusting from game to game. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/sports/mbball/roster/coaches/bill-self/40))
forecaster:
Kansas enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a profile that is more resilient than glamorous: a team that rates comfortably inside the national top 25 across the major systems, built on defense, schedule quality, and win equity more than on overwhelming offensive aesthetics. As of games through March 15, 2026, Kansas is No. 21 in the NCAA NET, No. 21 on KenPom, and No. 22 in ESPN BPI; Bart Torvik’s T-Rank also has the Jayhawks at No. 22. Their résumé metrics are better than those power ratings imply: Strength of Record is No. 18, KPI is No. 11, WAB is 16th, and their NET strength of schedule is No. 1 nationally. The record sits at 23-10 overall, including 14-2 at home, 5-6 away, and 4-2 on neutral floors, with a 9-9 record in Quad 1 and 7-1 in Quad 2. That is a classic high-exposure, high-difficulty Kansas tournament résumé. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/kansas-jayhawks))

The most important statistical tension in Kansas’s profile is this: the Jayhawks look like an elite defense attached to a merely good offense. RealGM’s 2025-26 advanced team page lists Kansas with a 110.0 offensive rating, a 90.3 defensive rating, and a +19.8 efficiency differential, while playing at a 68.5-possession pace. That defensive figure is the headline. It aligns with the broader public evidence: opponents are shooting just 38.5% from the field and 29.8% from three against Kansas through the March 4 team-stat update, and Bracketologists’ team sheet lists Kansas sixth nationally in field-goal percentage defense at 38.8%. In other words, the defense is not just “good for a contender”; it is the backbone of the team. ([basketball.realgm.com](https://basketball.realgm.com/ncaa/conferences/Big-12-Conference/3/Kansas/54/stats/2026/Advanced_Stats/All/Fr/November/PF/ortg/desc/1/))

On the offensive side, Kansas has been solid but not dominant. Through 30 games as of March 4, the Jayhawks were scoring 75.6 points per game and shooting 45.7% from the floor, 35.1% from three, and 77.2% at the foul line. Using those official totals, their estimated effective field-goal percentage is 51.96%, their turnover rate is about 13.8%, their offensive rebounding rate is about 29.2%, their free-throw rate is about 0.321, and their three-point attempt rate is about 0.357. Those are healthy, balanced offensive markers, but not the profile of an explosive, math-ball juggernaut. The ball security is especially useful in March: 322 turnovers against 1,762 field-goal attempts and 565 free-throw attempts indicates a team that generally gets shots up. But the shot-making efficiency itself is closer to “good national team” than “top-five offense.” ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/4/03032026_Kansas_Men_s_Basketball_Season_Stats.pdf))

If you want the cleaner advanced summary, Kansas is basically winning with shot suppression, sturdy half-court defense, and enough offensive competence to survive elite competition. RealGM’s split page shows opponent eFG% at just .405 overall, while Kansas posts a .546 eFG% of its own there; Bracketologists has the official public-facing effective field-goal mark at 51.6%, which is directionally consistent. The gap between those sources is likely methodological or date-based, but the core takeaway is unchanged: Kansas defends the arc extremely well, protects the paint well enough, and forces opponents into poor shooting nights more reliably than it overwhelms them with offensive firepower. ([basketball.realgm.com](https://basketball.realgm.com/ncaa/conferences/Big-12-Conference/3/Kansas/54/stats/2026/Advanced_Stats/All/Fr/November/PF/ortg/desc/1/))

Pace matters here because conventional wisdom still tends to imagine Kansas as a more up-tempo, talent-overwhelming team than this version actually is. At 68.5 possessions per 40 minutes, the Jayhawks are not slow-slow, but they are operating in a controlled range. This is a team more comfortable grinding quality possessions than racing into volatility. That fits the scoring profile: 75.6 points per game ranks only 178th nationally on the Bracketologists sheet, while scoring defense at 69.4 ranks 58th and raw field-goal defense is much stronger still. This is not a vintage Kansas offense that terrifies you every trip; it is a tournament team that can drag opponents into inefficient games. ([basketball.realgm.com](https://basketball.realgm.com/ncaa/conferences/Big-12-Conference/3/Kansas/54/stats/2026/Advanced_Stats/All/Fr/November/PF/ortg/desc/1/))

Recent form is mixed, and that is where the eye test and the spreadsheet start to diverge. Kansas entered late February having won nine of ten conference games, according to NCAA.com coverage, which suggests a strong upward trend before the finish. But the closing stretch also included a home blowout loss to Cincinnati, an 84-61 road loss at Arizona on February 28, and a 70-60 loss at Arizona State on March 3 in the official KU results log. So the macro trend says Kansas improved meaningfully in the heart of league play, while the immediate pre-tournament snapshot says the offense can still bog down badly against high-level or even simply competent resistance. That is not a contradiction so much as a warning label: Kansas’s median game is better than its ugly losses, but the ugly-loss tail is real. ([ncaa.com](https://www.ncaa.com/news/basketball-men/article/2026-02-21/cincinnati-hands-no-8-kansas-historic-loss-allen-fieldhouse?utm_source=openai))

The strength-of-schedule numbers help explain why the committee-facing résumé is stronger than some people’s visual impression. NET SOS at No. 1, RPI SOS at No. 2, and nonconference SOS marks in the mid-teens tell you Kansas played a brutally demanding slate. A 23-10 record with nine Quad 1 wins looks materially better in that context than the same record would on a softer schedule. This is also why Kansas can rate 21st-22nd in predictive systems while still carrying stronger résumé metrics like KPI 11 and SOR 18: the team has been stress-tested constantly, and it has accumulated enough quality results to offset the lack of dominant efficiency sparkle. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/kansas-jayhawks))

Where do the numbers depart from conventional wisdom? First, Kansas is more defense-first than brand perception suggests. The public still tends to associate the Jayhawks with star-driven shot creation and offensive fluidity, but the measurable edge is clearly on the defensive end. Second, the offense is cleaner than it looks in turnover terms but less dangerous than it looks in talent terms. A 13.8% turnover rate is strong, yet the eFG and 3-point volume are only moderately good, not elite. Third, the résumé is stronger than the raw record. With NET 21, KenPom 21, BPI 22, and the nation’s No. 1 NET SOS, Kansas looks like a team that can absolutely reach the second weekend if the shotmaking holds, but one that is less likely than a true top-10 contender to simply bomb opponents off the floor. ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/kansas-jayhawks))

Bottom line: Kansas projects as a dangerous but imperfect 2026 tournament team. The best case is obvious: an elite-caliber defense, solid rebounding, low offensive turnover rate, excellent free-throw shooting, and a résumé forged against the hardest schedule in the country. The concern is equally obvious: the offense has too many possessions where it is merely functional, and against teams that can score efficiently without turning it over, Kansas may not have enough easy offense to create separation. That combination makes the Jayhawks highly credible, but not invulnerable — more “high-floor, matchup-sensitive threat” than “steamrolling national-title favorite.” ([bracketologists.com](https://bracketologists.com/team/kansas-jayhawks))
matchup-analyst:
Kansas enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a defense-first, half-court-capable team that is still at its best when it can manufacture efficient transition chances off rebounds, blocks, and live-ball stops. Through March 4, Kansas was 21-9, allowing 2063 points in 30 games (68.8 per game) while scoring 2267 (75.6 per game). Before Big 12 play, Kansas was holding opponents to 36.6% from the field and 25.2% from three, while averaging 40.2 rebounds and 6.2 blocks per game; Flory Bidunga was at 14.7 points, 9.2 rebounds and 2.2 blocks per game, Darryn Peterson at 19.3 points in the four games he had played by Jan. 1, Tre White at 14.5 points and 7.0 rebounds, and Melvin Council Jr. was the primary table-setter with 67 assists and a 3.7 assist-to-turnover ratio at that point. By March 4, Peterson was up to 19.5 points per game in 19 games, White 14.0, Bidunga 14.9, and Tiller 8.5 with 6.0 rebounds. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/4/03032026_Kansas_Men_s_Basketball_Season_Stats.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Style of play: Kansas wants to defend, rebound, then score before the defense is set, but its overall tempo is not fast by national standards. SI’s KenPom-based review entering league play listed Kansas with a 92.6 adjusted defensive efficiency ranking ninth nationally while sitting outside the top 50 offensively; the same piece listed Kansas at 68.2 adjusted tempo, 212th nationally. On3 similarly reported Kansas ranked 256th in Division I in adjusted tempo and 236th in average possession length at that stage. That combination matters: Kansas is not a pure grind team by choice, but it is also not a high-possession pressure offense. If you take away the first 8-10 seconds and make them execute against a loaded half-court shell, their offense becomes much more vulnerable. ([si.com](https://www.si.com/college/kansas/basketball/what-kenpom-metrics-reveal-about-kansas-basketball-entering-big-12-play?utm_source=openai))

The specific tactics that disrupt Kansas are: 1) shrink the floor and force low-volume, late-clock threes; 2) pressure ball-handlers enough to deny early offense, but not so recklessly that Peterson and Council get downhill; 3) crowd Bidunga’s rolls with a low man and make non-creators finish; and 4) attack Kansas’s offense physically on the glass and through turnover conversion. Iowa State’s 74-56 win on February 14 is a clean example. Kansas shot only 19-of-51 overall, just 1-of-8 from three in the second half, and scored 56 total points. The Jayhawks produced 0 fast-break points, only 7 points off turnovers, and just 10 bench points, while Iowa State turned the game with 19 points off turnovers. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/boxscore.aspx?id=20339))

Press and zone vulnerability: I do not have a primary-source possession-type database from Synergy in the retrieved sources, so I cannot honestly claim an exact season-long press-offense or zone-offense PPP for 2025-26 Kansas. What the available game evidence does show is that teams that change coverages, flatten driving lanes, and force Kansas away from paint touches have had success. Arizona State beat Kansas 70-60 on March 3 even while shooting only 32.2% overall, because Kansas went 21-of-72 from the field, 7-of-27 from three, and committed 17 turnovers. Despite 17 Kansas fast-break points, the half-court offense bogged down badly; that is the profile of a team that could not consistently solve disruption once the game got ugly. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/boxscore.aspx?id=20336))

UCF’s 81-75 win on January 3 is another strong pressure/athleticism data point. Kansas scored 75 on decent efficiency, but UCF won the paint 38-30, bench 18-5, points off turnovers 15-8, and fast-break points were basically even at 15-16, which means UCF met Kansas’s transition game and still won by making the game more physical and deeper. Kansas also got only 2 points from Bryson Tiller and 5 total bench points. Against length and waves of athletes, the weak links in creation depth become visible. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/ucf/boxscore/20328))

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: Kansas clearly prefers a game where its defense creates quality run-outs, but not a chaotic 80-possession meet. When the Jayhawks got the game they wanted against Kansas State on March 7, they scored 104. When they got it against BYU on Jan. 31, game notes note 53 first-half points, 64.3% first-half shooting, and 11-of-22 from three overall in a 90-82 win. Kansas was also averaging 83.6 points in Big 12 play as of Feb. 1. But when opponents dragged them into lower-efficiency half-court possessions, results cratered: 56 against Iowa State, 61 at Arizona, 60 at Arizona State, and 47 against Houston in the Big 12 semifinals. To force the opposite of Kansas’s preferred environment, the opponent must send two back on the shot, limit live-ball turnovers, and make Kansas defend 20+ seconds repeatedly on the other end so Peterson and Council have to create late rather than attack advantage. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/2/1/KUMBB_Texas_Tech_notes.pdf))

Isolation vs. team offense tendencies: I cannot verify exact 2025-26 isolation percentage from a primary possession-type source in the retrieved material, so I will not invent one. What I can verify is that Kansas is a relatively assist-driven offense when functioning well. On Jan. 1 Kansas was averaging 15.8 assists per game, and on the season-through-March PDF key rotation players showed Council with 55 assists, White 55, Tiller 33, Jackson 45, and Peterson 31 despite only 19 games. That suggests the offense is better when multiple handlers move the ball and worse when it devolves into Peterson bailouts or late-clock individual creation. The Arizona State game is the warning sign: 60 points on 21-of-72 and 17 turnovers despite 14 offensive rebounds; they generated possessions but not clean team offense. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/news/2026/1/1/mens-basketball-no-17-kansas-opens-big-12-play-at-ucf-saturday))

Transition offense and defense frequency: I cannot verify exact season-long frequency percentages from a primary shot-type source in the retrieved material, but game-level evidence shows Kansas is dangerous when transition scoring is present and vulnerable when opponents either erase it or match it while winning other margins. Kansas had 16 fast-break points at UCF, 17 at Arizona State, and 9 against Houston in the Big 12 tournament loss; but Iowa State held them to 0 fast-break points in the 74-56 win. That is the clearest actionable split in the available evidence. If Kansas gets into the teens in fast-break scoring, the offense has a functional floor. If you hold them near zero and make them live in the half court, they can completely stall. Defensively, Kansas was elite early by percentage defense and blocks, but UCF still got 15 fast-break points and Arizona State turned 17 Kansas turnovers into 18 points off turnovers, so Kansas’s transition defense is most vulnerable after giveaways and bad shots, not necessarily after made baskets. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/sports/mens-basketball/stats/2025-26/ucf/boxscore/20328))

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: At the 5, Bidunga is the matchup problem Kansas imposes; he is 14.9 points per game on 68.6% shooting per ESPN’s team page snippet and 14.7/9.2 with 2.2 blocks in Kansas’s Jan. 1 notes. If your center cannot handle vertical rim pressure, lob coverage, and offensive rebounding, Kansas can play through him. At the wing, Tre White is the strength/production stabilizer at 14.0 points and 6.8 rebounds by March 4. Peterson is the star guard mismatch: 19.5 points per game by March 4, 26 at UCF in his return game, and real pull-up shot-making. Council is less explosive as a scorer but creates and rebounds from the guard spot. The vulnerability is the fourth/fifth offensive slots: Tiller was at 8.5 points with 57 turnovers by March 4, McDowell 3.7, Rosario 3.1 on 23.7% from three, and Jackson 4.7 on 36.4% shooting. Teams with multiple switchable wings can load onto Peterson/White/Council and test whether Tiller or the reserve guards can make enough jumpers and decisions. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/4/03032026_Kansas_Men_s_Basketball_Season_Stats.pdf))

Coaching adaptability: Bill Self’s staff still shows strong single-game bounce-back indicators. After losses, Kansas was 8-1 following a loss as of March 7, and 140-25 after a loss in the Bill Self era. That is not a playoff-series sample, but it is solid evidence of game-to-game adjustment quality. There is also role flexibility in the lineup: Kansas started different combinations late in the year, including Jayden Dawson, Wilder Evers, and Justin Cross in the March 7 win over Kansas State, which shows staff willingness to alter rotation structure. On the other hand, the repeated offensive collapses versus elite physical defenses - 56 vs Iowa State, 56 vs Houston on Feb. 23 even in a win, and 47 vs Houston on March 13 - suggest there are limits to in-game offensive counters when the first actions are removed. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/3/7/030726-PG-Notes-KSU.pdf?utm_source=openai))

Concrete game plan: To beat Kansas you must first kill the runway. Send two defenders back on every shot, value the ball, and force Kansas to score against a set half-court defense. Second, gap Peterson early and show bodies at Bidunga’s dives; make Kansas’s secondary shooters prove it over 40 minutes. Third, attack their offensive depth by switching size onto White and Council, then making Tiller, Rosario, McDowell, or Jackson finish possessions. Fourth, win the turnover-conversion battle: Iowa State got 19 points off Kansas turnovers, Arizona State got 18, and UCF got 15. Fifth, test Kansas’s half-court patience with coverage changes - man on one trip, packed gaps or zone principles the next - because the available evidence shows Kansas’s offense can become static and late-clock dependent. Sixth, make their bigs defend in space and make Peterson work defensively for a full clock, because Kansas’s slower overall tempo means extended defensive possessions also reduce the number of transition chances they can generate. Bottom line: if Kansas reaches 80 through ball movement and early offense, you probably lose; if you hold them below about 65 and erase their transition edge, the evidence from Iowa State, Arizona State, UCF, Arizona, and Houston says they are beatable. ([kuathletics.com](https://kuathletics.com/documents/download/2026/2/1/KUMBB_Texas_Tech_notes.pdf))
